query: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization but a low coercive field, and reported single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys derived from it have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe in the reported magnetic measurements. What single intervention could overcome this coercivity limitation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative, the relevant compositional, structural, and measurement boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor fraction of a heavy transition element with strong spin–orbit coupling, such as Ir, into equiatomic fcc FeCoNi will induce directional chemical ordering (e.g. L1_0-like ordering) while retaining a nominally single-phase microstructure. This ordering will lower the effective crystal symmetry, enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy, and thereby overcome the intrinsic coercivity limitation of <100 Oe found in the pure fcc FeCoNi system.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase face-centered cubic (fcc) FeCoNi alloy (e.g., equiatomic or near-equiatomic) exhibiting high saturation magnetization and coercivity below 100 Oe.
generation.intervention: Substitute approximately 10 atomic percent of one of the constituent elements with iridium (Ir) — forming an FeCoNi(Ir) alloy — to act as a single elemental intervention.
generation.conditions: Prepare thin films or bulk samples under conditions that favor a single-phase solid solution (e.g., sputtering or rapid solidification) at room temperature. Use standard alloy synthesis and heat treatments that do not otherwise induce multiphase decomposition.
generation.structural_mediator: Ir-induced local chemical ordering that promotes a low-symmetry (e.g. L1_0-like) ordering within the overall fcc lattice, without producing detectable secondary phases.
generation.mechanism: The heavy Ir atoms have strong spin–orbit coupling and a size/chemical mismatch relative to Fe, Co, and Ni. Their controlled incorporation is predicted to trigger directional chemical order and lattice distortions which lower the effective crystal symmetry. Consequently, the magnetocrystalline anisotropy is enhanced, thus increasing domain wall pinning and boosting coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coercive field is expected to increase by one to two orders of magnitude (e.g., rising from <100 Oe to several hundred Oe) relative to the baseline fcc FeCoNi, while the saturation magnetization remains comparably high.
generation.baseline: Coercivity measurements on single-phase fcc FeCoNi alloys (or matched derivatives) typically showing <100 Oe at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected when the Ir content is kept low (around 10 at.%) to ensure retention of a single-phase fcc matrix. Measurements should be conducted under room temperature conditions and within the compositional window where configurational entropy is still relatively high.
generation.uncertainty: The precise Ir concentration threshold required and the degree of induced ordering are uncertain. This hypothesis extrapolates from results with Pt addition (PMC11426066::web::002::introduction and PMC11426066::web::010::results_and_discussion) and extends their mechanism (directional ordering and enhanced spin–orbit coupling) to an alternative heavy element (Ir), a situation not previously fully explored.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of FeCoNi-based alloys with incremental Ir substitutions (e.g., 0%, 5%, 10%, and 15% Ir replacing a proportional amount of one of the base elements), ensuring homogeneous single-phase growth via sputtering or rapid solidification. Characterize the phase purity using X-ray diffraction (XRD) to confirm retention of the single-phase fcc structure and use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis. Magnetic properties will be measured at room temperature with a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM).
measurements: XRD patterns to verify that no secondary phases (e.g., complete L1_0 intermetallic phases with multiphase character) are formed
TEM micrographs to check for ordering and microstructural homogeneity
Hysteresis loops from VSM to determine coercivity (Hc) and saturation magnetization (Ms)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ir-substituted samples either (a) do not show a statistically significant increase in coercivity (i.e., Hc remains below ~100 Oe) or (b) produce detectable secondary phase formation (loss of single-phase fcc structure), then the hypothesis that a single Ir intervention can overcome the coercivity limitation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Most known HEAs fall in the category of soft magnetic materials, with coercivities below 100 Oe.[  ] However, coercivities as high as 1200 Oe have been reported in certain HEA systems.[  ] The coercivity is highly influenced by microstructure which may differ significantly amongst HEA systems depending on the fabrication conditions. The bulk of HEA studies focus predominantly on the maximum entropy solid solutions at the compositional center, which generally consist of uniform chemical disorder within cubic crystal structures, while low‐symmetry crystal structure and chemical order play an important role in magnetocrystalline anisotropy. However, it is not necessary that HEAs be fully disordered, as configurational entropy can be a dominant term in the free energy as long as the number of elements is large relative to the number of unique lattice sites.

The 1–2 orders of magnitude coercivity increase in RTA‐treated samples, compared to the as‐grown ones, suggests the emergence of sizeable magnetic anisotropy in the film. The fact that the continuous 15s RTA sample (Figure 1b) exhibits a 350 Oe coercivity, indicates that the dewetting process and film morphology evolution in some of the samples are not essential to the significant coercivity enhancement. Previous studies on bulk FeCoNiMnCu solid solutions have not found appreciable magnetic anisotropy ascribed to the disordered phase.[ ,  ] Hard magnetic properties in some solid solutions have been attributed to the magnetocrystalline or shape anisotropy of a secondary phase, however, studies of bulk phase‐separated FeCoNiMnCu have not shown large coercivity of the order presented here.[  ] In the present RTA‐treated samples, likely the anisotropic strain has induced lattice and grain distortions or directional chemical order, different from those in bulk systems, and stabilized sizable magnetic anisotropy, similar to that in RTA‐assisted synthesis of L10 FeCuPt.[ ,  ]
